story: In later Greek and Roman tellings, the sea goddess Thetis dipped her baby son Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel. That one untouched spot was where an arrow later struck and killed him at Troy.
def: a small but serious weakness in someone or something that is otherwise strong
ex: Priya is a brilliant surgeon, but her Achilles' heel is paperwork, which she always leaves until the last minute.
The team's defense is excellent; its Achilles' heel is a lack of speed on the counterattack.

cloze.s: Strong sales, low debt, loyal customers — the company's one ___ is that it depends on a single supplier.

story: In Greek myth, Pandora, the first woman, opened a jar that released sickness, toil, and other evils into the world; only hope remained inside. Later retellings turned the jar into a box.
def: an action that unleashes a whole series of unexpected problems that cannot be undone
ex: Changing the tax code without studying it first could open a Pandora's box of legal challenges.
Diego worried that asking about the old family feud would open Pandora's box at Thanksgiving dinner.

cloze.s: Once the city allowed one exception to the zoning rules, it opened a ___, and dozens of developers demanded the same treatment.

story: In Greek legend, after ten years of besieging Troy, the Greeks built a huge wooden horse, hid soldiers inside, and pretended to sail away. The Trojans brought the horse into their city, and that night the hidden soldiers opened the gates to the Greek army.
def: something that looks harmless or welcome but secretly brings in danger or an enemy from within
ex: The free app was a Trojan horse that quietly collected users' contacts and location data.
Critics called the small amendment a Trojan horse for much bigger changes to the law.

cloze.s: The friendly-looking email attachment was a ___: once opened, it let hackers into the hospital's network.

note: In computing, a “Trojan” is malicious software disguised as a useful program.

story: In Greek myth, King Midas of Phrygia was granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold. He soon regretted it when even his food turned to gold, and he begged to have the gift taken away.
def: the ability to make money or succeed at almost everything one attempts
ex: Kwame seems to have the Midas touch; every restaurant he opens is packed within a month.
The producer's Midas touch faded after three expensive flops in a row.

cloze.s: Investors lined up behind her new startup, convinced that her ___ would make it another success.

note: The myth is a warning about greed, but the modern phrase is usually admiring.

story: Hercules (Heracles in Greek) was the strongest of the Greek heroes. As penance he performed twelve famously difficult labors, such as killing the many-headed Hydra and capturing the three-headed dog Cerberus.
def: requiring enormous strength, effort, or determination; extremely hard to accomplish
ex: Cleaning up the flooded basement was a Herculean job that took the whole family two weekends.
Wei made a Herculean effort to finish her nursing degree while working night shifts.

cloze.s: Rebuilding the bridge in just three months would take a ___ effort from every crew in the region.

story: Cupid was the Roman god of love, usually shown as a winged boy with a bow. Anyone struck by one of his arrows fell in love.
def: to try to bring two people together romantically; act as a matchmaker
ex: Aisha played Cupid by seating her two single friends next to each other at her wedding.
Grandpa loves to play Cupid, always mentioning the nice young doctor down the street.

cloze.s: Malik decided to ___ and invited both of his lonely coworkers to the same dinner party.

story: In a parable told by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke, a man is robbed and left injured by the road. A priest and a Levite pass him by, but a Samaritan, from a group the listeners were hostile toward, stops, treats his wounds, and pays for his care.
def: a stranger who helps someone in trouble without expecting anything in return
ex: A good Samaritan changed Olga's flat tire on the highway and drove off before she could thank him.
Many states have laws protecting good Samaritans who give first aid at accident scenes.

cloze.s: When the elderly man collapsed at the bus stop, a ___ called 911 and stayed with him until help arrived.

story: In the Hebrew Bible (1 Samuel), the young shepherd David faces Goliath, a giant Philistine warrior. Armed only with a sling and stones, David strikes Goliath in the forehead and defeats him.
def: a contest in which a small, weak side faces a far larger, more powerful opponent
ex: The lawsuit between the family bakery and the global food company was a classic David and Goliath battle.
Fans loved the David and Goliath story of the tiny college beating the national champions.

cloze.s: The small-town newspaper's fight against the media giant was a true ___ struggle, and readers rooted for the underdog.

story: In the Book of Genesis, God tells Adam and Eve they may eat from any tree in the Garden of Eden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Tempted by a serpent, they eat its fruit and are driven out of the garden.
def: something desired all the more because it is not allowed or is considered wrong
ex: For the teenagers, the locked liquor cabinet was forbidden fruit, which only made it more tempting.
Dessert became forbidden fruit for Tomás once his doctor told him to cut back on sugar.

cloze.s: Because her parents banned video games, they became a kind of ___ that Yuki thought about constantly.

note: Genesis never says the fruit was an apple; that idea came later in European tradition.

story: In the Book of Leviticus, on the Day of Atonement the high priest symbolically placed the sins of the people on a goat, which was then sent away into the wilderness, carrying their sins with it.
def: a person or group unfairly blamed for problems or mistakes that others caused
ex: The intern became the scapegoat for a software failure that was really caused by the manager's rushed deadline.
History shows that in hard times, minorities are often made scapegoats for economic problems.

cloze.s: Rather than admit the plan was flawed, the coach made the rookie goalie the ___ for the loss.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus teaches that if someone strikes you on the right cheek, you should turn the other to them as well, rather than seeking revenge.
def: to respond to an insult or attack calmly, without striking back or seeking revenge
ex: When a rival posted mean comments about her, Hannah turned the other cheek and simply ignored them.
It's hard to turn the other cheek when a coworker takes credit for your work.

cloze.s: Instead of shouting back at the rude driver, Jamal chose to ___ and drove on.

story: This principle of equal punishment appears in the laws of the Hebrew Bible (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the even older Code of Hammurabi. Jesus later quotes it in the Sermon on the Mount, urging forgiveness instead.
def: the idea that punishment or revenge should match the harm that was done
ex: The debate over the death penalty often comes down to whether justice means an eye for an eye.
Fatima told her sons that an eye for an eye just keeps a fight going forever.

cloze.s: The two neighbors lived by ___: when one blasted music late at night, the other did the same the next evening.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus says that if someone forces you to go one mile, you should go with them two. The saying came to mean doing more than is required.
def: to make more effort than is expected or required of you
ex: The hotel staff went the extra mile, leaving a birthday cake in our room after overhearing us.
Liam always goes the extra mile for his students, staying late to help anyone who's struggling.

cloze.s: Customers keep coming back because the shop's employees ___, even delivering orders on their way home.

term: by the skin of your teeth
story: The phrase comes from the Book of Job in the King James Bible, where the suffering Job says, “I am escaped with the skin of my teeth,” describing how narrowly he has survived.
def: only just; by the narrowest possible margin
ex: Sofia passed her driving test by the skin of her teeth, scraping through with the minimum score.
We caught the last train home by the skin of our teeth, jumping on as the doors closed.

cloze.s: Diego and Maria made their connecting flight ___, sprinting up to the gate just before it shut.
cloze.a: by the skin of their teeth

story: In Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, karma is the principle that a person's intentional actions shape their future experiences, including future lives in the cycle of rebirth.
def: the idea that good or bad actions eventually bring matching consequences back to the person who did them
ex: He cut in line and then spilled coffee all over himself — instant karma, Olga joked.
Priya believes that good karma comes from treating everyone with kindness.

cloze.s: After years of helping neighbors, Kwame felt it was ___ when a stranger returned his lost wallet with every dollar inside.

note: Everyday English often treats it as quick payback or luck; in its original traditions it is a long-term moral law that can span lifetimes.

story: In Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism, a guru is a spiritual teacher or guide; the word is Sanskrit. In Sikhism, the title belongs to the ten founding Gurus and to the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib.
def: an expert or trusted adviser in a particular field whom others look to for guidance
ex: The company hired a marketing guru to help relaunch its tired brand.
Ask Jamal about your phone settings — he's the tech guru of the family.

cloze.s: Thousands of investors hang on every word of the self-styled financial ___, who claims his system never fails.

note: In its religious sense the word carries deep reverence; in casual English it can sound playful or mocking (“a self-styled guru”).

story: In one of Aesop's fables, a fox tries again and again to reach a bunch of grapes hanging high on a vine. When he fails, he walks away saying they were probably sour anyway.
def: pretending to dislike or look down on something only because you could not get it yourself
ex: When Liam said he never wanted the promotion anyway, everyone knew it was sour grapes.
The losing team's complaints about the referees sounded like sour grapes to most fans.

cloze.s: Calling the award “meaningless” right after losing it sounded like ___ to the other nominees.

story: In Aesop's fable “The Boy Who Cried Wolf,” a shepherd boy repeatedly fools villagers by shouting that a wolf is attacking his flock. When a wolf really comes, no one believes him.
def: to raise false alarms so often that people stop believing you when a real problem comes
ex: Maria has cried wolf about quitting so many times that her boss no longer takes it seriously.
If the weather service keeps issuing storm warnings that never pan out, it risks crying wolf.

cloze.s: Our smoke detector goes off every time we make toast, and I worry it's ___ so often that we'll ignore a real fire.

term: slow and steady wins the race
story: In Aesop's fable “The Tortoise and the Hare,” a speedy hare mocks a slow tortoise and agrees to race it. The overconfident hare naps along the way, and the tortoise, plodding on without stopping, crosses the finish line first.
def: consistent, patient effort usually succeeds better than speed combined with carelessness or overconfidence
ex: Aisha paid off her student loans a little each month, proving that slow and steady wins the race.
When it comes to losing weight safely, slow and steady wins the race.

cloze.s: Wei's coach reminded her that in a marathon, ___, so she shouldn't sprint the first mile.
cloze.a: slow and steady wins the race

story: In Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale “The Ugly Duckling,” a homely young bird is teased by the ducks and other animals. After a hard winter it grows up and discovers it is actually a beautiful swan.
def: someone or something considered unattractive or unpromising at first that later becomes impressive or beautiful
ex: The run-down warehouse was the ugly duckling of the block until artists turned it into a gallery.
Tomás was the ugly duckling of his class but grew into a confident, striking adult.

cloze.s: Once the plainest car in the lineup, the boxy hatchback turned out to be the ___ that became the company's bestseller.

story: In the folk tale of Cinderella, best known from the versions by Charles Perrault and the Brothers Grimm, a mistreated young woman forced to work for her stepfamily gets magical help to attend a royal ball and ends up marrying the prince.
def: an unexpected success by an unknown or overlooked person or team that rises from obscurity to fame
ex: The low-ranked college's run to the championship game was the Cinderella story of the tournament.
Her rise from mailroom clerk to company president is a real Cinderella story.

cloze.s: No one expected the unknown singer from a small town to win the national contest, making hers the ___ of the season.

story: In the English folk tale “The Three Little Pigs,” a wolf blows down the houses that two pigs built of straw and sticks but cannot blow down the third pig's house of bricks. A 1933 Disney cartoon made “Big Bad Wolf” a familiar label.
def: a person or thing portrayed as a frightening villain or threat, often more than it deserves
ex: Local shop owners treat the new superstore as the big bad wolf that will drive them out of business.
In the movie, the greedy landlord is the big bad wolf who threatens to evict everyone.

cloze.s: Some economists argue that automation isn't the ___ it's made out to be and will create new jobs.

story: In Old Norse sagas and poems, berserkers were warriors said to fight in a wild, trancelike fury, seemingly unaware of pain or danger.
def: to become wildly out of control with anger, excitement, or frenzy
ex: The crowd went berserk when the home team scored in the final second.
Our dog goes berserk every time the mail carrier walks up the driveway.

cloze.s: When the store announced a 90 percent off sale, shoppers ___ and rushed the doors.

story: Homer's epic poem the Odyssey tells of the Greek hero Odysseus's ten-year journey home after the Trojan War, full of monsters, storms, and detours.
def: a long, eventful journey or experience full of adventures and changes of fortune
ex: Getting a visa turned into a six-month bureaucratic odyssey for Malik's family.
Their road trip became an odyssey of flat tires, wrong turns, and unforgettable diners.

cloze.s: After three canceled flights and a night in a bus station, Hannah's trip home had become a true ___.

story: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution, who punished people for arrogance and excessive pride, especially toward the gods.
def: a long-standing rival or enemy who is hard to defeat, or something that keeps causing someone's downfall
ex: The chess champion finally beat her old nemesis after losing to him five years in a row.
Math was Kwame's nemesis all through high school.

cloze.s: The rival school had beaten them every year for a decade, so the coach called it the team's ___.

story: In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor is the old friend Odysseus leaves in charge of his household, and the goddess Athena takes Mentor's form to guide Odysseus's young son, Telemachus. A popular 1699 French novel about Telemachus helped make the name a word for a wise guide.
def: an experienced, trusted person who advises and guides someone less experienced over time
ex: Dr. Patel became Yuki's mentor during residency, teaching her far more than any textbook.
The program pairs each new employee with a mentor from another department.

cloze.s: Throughout her first year of teaching, Maria met weekly with her ___, a veteran teacher who helped her plan lessons.

story: In Greek myth, the Sirens were creatures whose beautiful singing lured sailors to wreck their ships on the rocks. In the Odyssey, Odysseus has his crew plug their ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast so he can hear the song safely.
def: a tempting appeal that is hard to resist but likely to lead to trouble or ruin
ex: Many investors fell for the siren song of quick profits and lost their savings.
Sofia resisted the siren song of the sofa and went for her evening run.

cloze.s: Despite promising to save money, Diego couldn't resist the ___ of the holiday sales and maxed out his credit card.

story: In Greek myth, the Titans were a race of giant, powerful gods who ruled before Zeus and the Olympian gods overthrew them.
def: a person of enormous power, importance, or achievement, especially in business or a particular field
ex: The museum was funded by a steel titan of the early 1900s.
When the two tech titans met in court, the case drew worldwide attention.

cloze.s: As a ___ of the shipping industry, she controlled ports on three continents.

story: In Ovid's version of the Greek myth, the beautiful young man Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection in a pool and wastes away gazing at it; a flower that bears his name grows where he died.
def: a person excessively absorbed in themselves who craves admiration and shows little real concern for others
ex: Her ex was such a narcissist that every conversation somehow ended up being about him.
The talk-show host came across as a narcissist, constantly steering questions back to his own career.

cloze.s: Liam realized his new boss was a ___ when she took credit for the team's work and demanded constant praise.

note: Also a clinical term (narcissistic personality disorder); in everyday speech it is often used loosely as an insult.

story: In ancient legend, told by Greek and Roman writers, the phoenix was a sacred bird that lived for centuries and then was reborn; in the best-known version it bursts into flames and rises again from its own ashes.
def: a person or thing that makes a powerful comeback after being destroyed or seeming finished
ex: After the fire, the bakery rose like a phoenix from the ashes, reopening bigger than before.
Critics hailed the singer as a phoenix after a comeback album that many had thought impossible.

cloze.s: The bankrupt airline seemed finished, but under new owners it rose like a ___ from the ashes.

term: fly too close to the sun
story: In Greek myth, the craftsman Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax so he and his son Icarus could escape Crete. Icarus ignored his father's warning, flew too close to the sun, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea.
def: to become dangerously overambitious or reckless and suffer disaster as a result
ex: The founder flew too close to the sun, expanding into ten countries before the business could support it.
Olga's coach warned her not to fly too close to the sun by training through injuries.

cloze.s: Analysts said the hedge fund had ___ by borrowing huge sums on a single risky bet.
cloze.a: flown too close to the sun

story: In a parable told by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke, a younger son wastes his inheritance in reckless living, then returns home in shame. His father joyfully welcomes him back and throws a feast, to the resentment of the dutiful older brother.
def: a person who leaves home or a group, behaves irresponsibly, and later returns regretful and is welcomed back
ex: When the star player rejoined his first club after years abroad, fans hailed the return of the prodigal son.
Jamal felt like the prodigal son, coming home broke after his failed music career.

cloze.s: After a decade of ignoring the family, Uncle Ray showed up at the reunion, and Grandma welcomed him like the ___.

note: Prodigal alone means wastefully extravagant; it does not mean “returning,” a common misunderstanding.

story: In the Gospel of John, the apostle Thomas refuses to believe the other disciples' report that Jesus has risen until he can see and touch the wounds himself.
def: a person who refuses to believe something without direct, personal proof
ex: Even after seeing the test results, a few doubting Thomases on the board wanted another study.
Don't be a doubting Thomas; the bus really does stop right outside the hotel.

cloze.s: Aisha was the office ___, refusing to believe the new software worked until she tested it herself.

story: In the Gospels, Judas Iscariot, one of Jesus's twelve apostles, betrayed him to the authorities for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss.
def: a person who betrays a friend or ally, especially someone who pretends to be loyal
ex: Fans called the striker a Judas when he signed with their bitterest rivals.
She felt she'd been betrayed by a Judas when her business partner sold their idea to a competitor.

cloze.s: After leaking the team's plans to a rival company, Mark was branded a ___ by his former colleagues.

story: In the Book of Daniel, during a feast held by King Belshazzar of Babylon, a mysterious hand writes words on the palace wall. Daniel interprets them as a sign that the king's reign is ending, and Belshazzar is killed that night.
def: clear signs that something bad, such as failure or an ending, is about to happen
ex: When the store cut its hours and stopped restocking, employees saw the writing on the wall.
The writing was on the wall for the old factory once its biggest customer moved overseas.

cloze.s: After three straight losing seasons and empty stands, the coach could read ___ and resigned.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus tells his followers, “Ye are the salt of the earth,” praising them as valuable and good for the world.
def: a decent, honest, unpretentious person who is kind and dependable
ex: Our neighbors are salt of the earth; they shoveled our driveway every morning while I was in the hospital.
The farmer was the salt of the earth, always the first to help anyone in town.

cloze.s: Everyone at the funeral agreed that Grandpa Tomás was ___, a hardworking man who never had an unkind word.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus warns against false prophets “which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
def: someone who hides harmful intentions behind a friendly, innocent appearance
ex: The charming financial adviser turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing who stole his clients' savings.
Be careful with that “friendly” new landlord; he might be a wolf in sheep's clothing.

cloze.s: Police warned seniors that the polite caller offering free repairs was a ___ running a scam.

story: In the Book of Revelation, Armageddon is named as the place where the kings of the world gather for a final battle at the end of time. The name is usually traced to Megiddo, an ancient city in present-day Israel.
def: a catastrophic final conflict or disaster, especially one that seems to threaten everything
ex: Shoppers stripped the shelves before the storm as if preparing for Armageddon.
Analysts warned that a full trade war would mean economic Armageddon for small exporters.

cloze.s: The movie imagines a nuclear ___ that leaves only a few survivors scattered across the globe.

story: In Buddhism, nirvana is the final goal of spiritual practice: release from craving and suffering and from the cycle of rebirth. The Sanskrit word means “blowing out,” as of a flame; the idea also appears in Hinduism and Jainism.
def: a state of perfect happiness, peace, or satisfaction; an ideal place or condition
ex: For a coffee lover like Kwame, the tiny café in Rome was pure nirvana.
A quiet beach with no phone signal is Priya's idea of nirvana.

cloze.s: After months of construction noise next door, the silent cabin in the woods felt like pure ___ to Hannah.

note: The everyday sense (bliss, paradise) is much looser than the Buddhist meaning, which is liberation from desire and rebirth, not pleasure.

story: In Hinduism and Buddhism, a mantra is a sacred word, sound, or phrase, often in Sanskrit, repeated in prayer or meditation; “om” is a well-known example.
def: a slogan or principle someone repeats often because it sums up their beliefs or approach
ex: “Customer first” is the mantra repeated at every staff meeting.
Wei's mantra during the last miles of the marathon was simply, “One more step.”

cloze.s: “Location, location, location” is the ___ of every real estate agent.

note: Everyday English uses it for any often-repeated motto; originally it means a sacred utterance used in worship or meditation.

story: In Hinduism, an avatar (Sanskrit avatara, “descent”) is an earthly form taken by a god; Rama and Krishna are revered as avatars of the god Vishnu.
def: an embodiment of an idea or quality, or a figure that represents a person in a game or online
ex: To his fans, the guitarist was the avatar of rock-and-roll rebellion.
Yuki chose a purple dragon as her avatar in the online game.

cloze.s: Before joining the video call, Diego picked a cartoon ___ to represent him on screen.

note: The original sense is religious; the computing sense spread from the 1980s and 1990s.

story: Zen is a school of Mahayana Buddhism that developed in China (where it is called Chan) and spread to Japan, emphasizing meditation and direct insight over the study of texts.
def: (informal) calm, peaceful, and unbothered, especially in a stressful situation
ex: Despite the screaming toddlers on the plane, Sofia stayed totally Zen.
Malik's minimalist apartment has a very Zen feel, with bare walls and soft light.

cloze.s: Even when the server crashed on launch day, our project lead remained completely ___ and calmly fixed it.

note: This casual sense (often lowercase, “so zen”) is far looser than the Buddhist tradition it comes from.

story: Mecca, in Saudi Arabia, is the holiest city in Islam: the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, the site of the Kaaba, toward which Muslims pray, and the destination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage.
def: a place that attracts many people who share a particular interest or activity
ex: Nashville has long been a mecca for aspiring country musicians.
With dozens of trails, the mountain town is a Mecca for serious bikers.

cloze.s: With its famous museums and studios, the city became a ___ for young artists from around the world.

note: Often written lowercase in this sense. Some people find the casual use insensitive, so “hub” or “magnet” are safe alternatives.

story: In Hans Christian Andersen's tale, swindlers sell a vain emperor “clothes” they claim are invisible to anyone stupid or unfit for office. No one dares admit seeing nothing until a child in the crowd cries out that the emperor has nothing on.
def: something widely praised that everyone pretends to admire, though it is actually worthless or fake
ex: Some critics say the hyped cryptocurrency is just the emperor's new clothes.
The blank canvas priced at a million dollars struck Jamal as a case of the emperor's new clothes.

cloze.s: Everyone in the meeting praised the confusing strategy until an intern pointed out that it was a case of ___.

story: In “Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves,” a tale added to the Arabian Nights by its 18th-century French translator Antoine Galland, the words “Open, Sesame!” magically open the thieves' treasure cave.
def: something that gives easy, almost automatic access to an opportunity or goal that is otherwise hard to reach
ex: A degree from that university used to be an open sesame to high-paying jobs.
For the young chef, winning the competition was an open sesame to the best kitchens in Paris.

cloze.s: In that industry, knowing the right people is the ___ that gets you hired.

story: The phrase comes from the Book of Isaiah, which condemns hypocrites who say, “Come not near to me; for I am holier than thou,” as the King James Bible renders it.
def: smugly acting morally superior to other people; self-righteous
ex: Liam's holier-than-thou attitude about recycling annoyed his roommates.
The celebrity's holier-than-thou posts about saving energy backfired when photos of her private jet surfaced.

cloze.s: Nobody likes the ___ coworker who lectures everyone about healthy eating while sneaking candy at her desk.

story: In Greek myth, the nine Muses were goddesses, daughters of Zeus, who inspired poetry, music, history, dance, and the other arts; ancient poets often opened their works by calling on a Muse.
def: a person or thing that inspires an artist, writer, or musician to create
ex: The painter's wife was his lifelong muse, appearing in dozens of his portraits.
For Aisha, the city's rainy streets are a constant muse for her songwriting.

cloze.s: The novelist said her grandmother's stories were the ___ behind every book she wrote.

story: In Greek myth, Cassandra, a princess of Troy, was given the gift of prophecy by the god Apollo, but after she rejected him he cursed her so that no one would believe her. Her warnings about the fall of Troy were ignored.
def: a person who correctly predicts disaster but whose warnings are dismissed or ignored
ex: The economist who warned about the housing bubble was treated as a Cassandra until it burst.
Olga felt like a Cassandra, warning about the leaky roof for months before the ceiling collapsed.

cloze.s: For years, the scientist was dismissed as a ___, but the flood she predicted arrived exactly as she said.

note: Unlike a Chicken Little, whose alarms are false, a Cassandra turns out to be right.

story: In Greek myth, King Sisyphus was punished in the underworld by being forced to roll a huge boulder up a hill, only for it to roll back down every time it neared the top, forever.
def: endless, exhausting, and ultimately futile, like a task that must be repeated without ever being finished
ex: Keeping the beach clean felt Sisyphean, as each tide washed up new trash.
Answering email can be a Sisyphean chore: clear the inbox and it fills up again within an hour.

cloze.s: With two toddlers, keeping the living room tidy is a ___ task that starts over the moment she finishes.

note: Herculean means hugely difficult but achievable; Sisyphean means never-ending and pointless.

story: In Greek myth, King Tantalus was punished in the underworld by standing in water that drained away whenever he bent to drink, beneath fruit branches that swung out of reach whenever he grabbed for them.
def: to tease or torment someone by showing them something desirable that they cannot have
ex: The smell of fresh bread from the bakery tantalized commuters waiting at the bus stop.
The trailer tantalized fans with a brief glimpse of the long-awaited sequel.

cloze.s: The menu ___ the hungry hikers with pictures of burgers, but the kitchen had already closed for the night.

story: In Greek myth, the craftsman Daedalus built the Labyrinth, a maze on Crete, for King Minos to imprison the Minotaur. The hero Theseus killed the monster and found his way out by following a thread given to him by Ariadne.
def: extremely complicated and confusing, like a maze, whether in physical layout or in procedures
ex: The hospital's labyrinthine corridors left visitors wandering for twenty minutes.
Fatima spent weeks navigating the labyrinthine rules for her small-business loan.

cloze.s: The old city's ___ alleys twist and turn so much that even locals sometimes get lost.

story: In ancient Greece, an oracle was a shrine where a god was believed to answer questions through a priest or priestess; the most famous was at Delphi, where Apollo's priestess, the Pythia, delivered prophecies.
def: a person considered a source of wise, authoritative advice or reliable predictions
ex: On anything involving baseball statistics, Diego is the family oracle.
Investors treated the veteran fund manager as an oracle, hanging on her every forecast.

cloze.s: In her village, the old almanac was treated like ___: no one planted a single crop without consulting its predictions.

story: In Greek myth, Adonis was a young man of extraordinary beauty loved by Aphrodite, the goddess of love. He was killed by a wild boar while hunting.
def: an extremely handsome and attractive young man, often one with an athletic build
ex: The new lifeguard was such an Adonis that half the beach seemed to be watching him.
In the ad, a bronzed Adonis strolls along the shore wearing the brand's sunglasses.

cloze.s: The sculptor's marble statue of a muscular, strikingly handsome young ___ draws crowds of admiring visitors.

story: In the Gospel of John, a crowd brings a woman accused of adultery to Jesus and asks whether she should be stoned. He replies, “He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her,” and the accusers leave one by one.
def: to be the first to criticize or blame someone, especially when you are not blameless yourself
ex: Before you cast the first stone at Liam for being late, remember you missed the last two meetings.
None of the other teams can cast the first stone; they all broke the same practice rules.

cloze.s: We've all made mistakes with money, so I'm not going to ___ just because my brother overspent.

story: The phrase echoes the Book of Isaiah, where, compared with God's greatness, “the nations are as a drop of a bucket,” as the King James Bible puts it.
def: an amount so small that it makes almost no difference compared with what is needed
ex: The fifty-dollar donation felt like a drop in the bucket compared to the clinic's huge debts.
Planting a few trees is a drop in the bucket, but Sofia says every bit helps.

cloze.s: The city's $2 million grant is ___ next to the billions needed to repair its bridges.

story: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus describes certain religious leaders as blind guides and says, “if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.”
def: a situation where people with no knowledge or skill are guiding others who know just as little
ex: With two brand-new hires training each other, it was the blind leading the blind.
Hannah laughed that her dad teaching her to use the new phone was the blind leading the blind.

cloze.s: Neither tour guide had ever been to the city before, so the walk was a case of ___.

story: In the Hebrew Bible, God promises the land of Canaan to Abraham and his descendants; in Exodus, Moses leads the Israelites out of Egypt and through the wilderness toward it.
def: a place or situation where someone expects to find happiness, success, or a better life
ex: For many 19th-century immigrants, America was the promised land.
Reaching the championship was the promised land the club had chased for decades.

cloze.s: For the struggling minor-league player, a contract with a big-league team was the ___ he had dreamed of reaching for years.

story: The Book of Exodus tells how Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, a mass departure that gave the book its name (Greek for “going out”).
def: a mass departure of many people at once from a place, company, or group
ex: The factory closure led to an exodus of young families from the town.
There was an exodus of fans from the stadium once the home team fell behind by thirty points.

cloze.s: When the new CEO cut bonuses, a sudden ___ of senior engineers left the company short-staffed.

story: In a parable in the Gospel of Matthew, a landowner hires workers throughout the day, including some at the eleventh hour, just before work ends, and pays them the same as those who started at dawn.
def: at the last possible moment, just before it is too late
ex: The deal was saved at the eleventh hour when both sides agreed to split the costs.
Jamal always starts his term papers at the eleventh hour and stays up all night.

cloze.s: Our roommate only ever does his share of the chores ___, minutes before the landlord's inspection.

story: In Genesis, God destroys the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah by raining down “brimstone and fire” (brimstone is sulfur), and the Book of Revelation describes a lake of fire and brimstone as punishment for the wicked.
def: stern, frightening warnings of punishment for wrongdoing, especially in angry preaching or speeches
ex: The pastor was known for fire-and-brimstone sermons about the evils of gambling.
The coach's fire-and-brimstone halftime speech woke the team up.

cloze.s: The principal delivered a ___ lecture, warning that anyone caught cheating would be expelled immediately.

story: Under Jewish dietary laws, which come from the Torah and later rabbinic tradition, food that is kosher (Hebrew for “fit” or “proper”) is permitted to eat, such as meat from certain animals slaughtered in a prescribed way.
def: (informal) legitimate, proper, or acceptable according to the rules
ex: Before signing, Priya asked her lawyer whether the contract terms were kosher.
Combining a coupon with the store discount isn't kosher at that shop, the cashier explained.

cloze.s: The auditor wanted to make sure the company's accounting was completely ___ before approving the annual report.

note: This casual sense is borrowed from the religious one; in its original meaning, kosher refers to food and practices that meet Jewish law.

story: In ancient Chinese philosophy, especially Daoism, yin (dark, cool, receptive) and yang (bright, warm, active) are opposite but complementary forces whose balance and interplay make up everything in the universe.
def: two opposite but complementary forces, people, or qualities that balance each other out
ex: Maria is calm and Diego is excitable; their friendship is a perfect yin and yang.
The restaurant's menu balances spicy and cooling dishes like yin and yang.

cloze.s: The quiet engineer and the outgoing salesman were the ___ of the startup, each supplying what the other lacked.

story: The word comes from Jagannath, a form of the Hindu god Vishnu worshipped at Puri, India, whose image is pulled through the streets on huge chariots during the yearly Rath Yatra festival. Early European travelers' accounts, often exaggerated, of devotees crushed beneath the wheels gave English its sense of an unstoppable force.
def: a huge, powerful force or organization that crushes everything in its path and seems unstoppable
ex: The online retailer has become a juggernaut that small shops struggle to compete with.
Streaming services became a juggernaut that drove video rental stores out of business.

cloze.s: The undefeated champions rolled over every opponent like an unstoppable ___.

story: Jewish and Islamic traditions describe seven heavens, one above another; the seventh, the highest, is the closest to God, so being “in seventh heaven” came to mean perfect bliss.
def: a state of extreme happiness and delight
ex: With a new puppy and a week off school, Yuki was in seventh heaven.
Grandpa was in seventh heaven when all eleven grandkids showed up for his birthday.

cloze.s: The surprise tickets to see her favorite band put Hannah in ___ for the rest of the week.

term: kill the goose that lays the golden eggs
story: In Aesop's fable, a farmer owns a goose that lays a golden egg each day. Greedy for all the gold at once, he kills the goose and cuts it open, only to find nothing inside, and loses his source of wealth.
def: to destroy a reliable source of profit or benefit through greed or impatience
ex: Raising fees too sharply could kill the goose that lays the golden eggs for the city's tourism industry.
Cutting the research budget to boost short-term profit is killing the goose that lays the golden eggs.

cloze.s: If the landlord triples the rent, his best tenant will move out and he'll ___.
cloze.a: kill the goose that lays the golden eggs

story: In a German legend recorded by the Brothers Grimm and retold in a poem by Robert Browning, a piper in colorful clothes rids the town of Hamelin of rats by luring them away with his music. When the town refuses to pay him, he plays again and leads away its children, who are never seen again.
def: a charismatic person who attracts many followers, often with promises that lead them into trouble
ex: The self-help influencer became a Pied Piper for thousands who bought his useless courses.
The ice cream truck's jingle made its driver the Pied Piper of the neighborhood kids.

cloze.s: Like a modern ___, the charismatic speaker led crowds of young investors into a scheme that collapsed.

story: In English folk legends dating back to the Middle Ages, Robin Hood is an outlaw of Sherwood Forest who, in the best-known versions, robs the rich to help the poor.
def: a person who takes from the wealthy, sometimes illegally, to help those in need
ex: The bank robber became a folk hero, a Robin Hood who reportedly gave cash to struggling farmers.
Fans romanticized the hacker as a Robin Hood, but he kept most of the stolen money himself.

cloze.s: The thief was nicknamed the neighborhood's ___ because he stole from luxury stores and gave the goods to homeless shelters.

story: In medieval legends of King Arthur, the knights of the Round Table set out on a quest for the Holy Grail, a sacred vessel identified in later versions with the cup Jesus used at the Last Supper. Only the purest knight could achieve it.
def: something extremely desirable that people search for intensely but that is very hard to obtain
ex: A cure for the common cold remains the holy grail of virus research.
For collectors, a mint-condition 1952 baseball card is the holy grail.

cloze.s: For battery engineers, a cheap cell that fully charges in one minute is the ___ of the industry.

note: Usually written lowercase in this figurative sense.

story: In Charles Perrault's version of the Cinderella tale, Cinderella's fairy godmother uses magic to give her a coach, horses, a gown, and glass slippers so she can attend the royal ball.
def: a generous helper who unexpectedly appears and solves someone's problems or makes their wishes come true
ex: An anonymous donor played fairy godmother, paying off the school's entire lunch debt.
Aunt Olga was Tomás's fairy godmother, covering his college tuition when his scholarship fell through.

cloze.s: When a local business owner surprised the band with new instruments, the students called her their ___.

story: In an old folk tale, Chicken Little (also called Henny Penny) is hit on the head by a falling acorn and panics, convinced that “the sky is falling,” and rushes off to warn the king, spreading alarm among the other animals.
def: a person who panics and warns that disaster is coming without good reason
ex: The analyst has predicted a crash every year for a decade, earning him a reputation as a Chicken Little.
Don't be a Chicken Little; one bad quarter doesn't mean the company is doomed.

cloze.s: Every time the stock market dips, my uncle plays ___, shouting that the sky is falling.

note: Contrast Cassandra, whose warnings turn out to be true.

term: the genie is out of the bottle
story: In “The Fisherman and the Jinni,” a tale from the Arabian Nights (One Thousand and One Nights), a fisherman opens a sealed brass jar pulled from the sea and releases a huge, dangerous jinni (genie) who had been imprisoned inside.
def: something powerful, often harmful, has been released and can no longer be controlled or reversed
ex: Once the technology was shared online, the genie was out of the bottle.
Releasing the secret files let the genie out of the bottle, and the scandal grew by the hour.

cloze.s: Now that cheap drones are everywhere, ___, and no law can make them disappear.
cloze.a: the genie is out of the bottle

note: Close to Pandora's box, but stresses that the change cannot be undone rather than that troubles multiply.

story: In the English tale “Goldilocks and the Three Bears,” a girl enters the bears' empty house and tries their porridge, chairs, and beds, rejecting each one that is too hot or too cold, too hard or too soft, until she finds one that is “just right.”
def: describing a condition that is neither too much nor too little, but balanced and just right
ex: Economists described a Goldilocks economy, growing steadily without driving up inflation.
Astronomers search for planets in the Goldilocks zone, where water could stay liquid.

cloze.s: The apartment was a ___ choice for Wei: not too far from work, not too expensive, and not too small.

story: In a fable credited to Aesop, a lion goes hunting with other animals and, when the prey is divided, claims every portion for himself with one excuse or threat after another.
def: the largest part of something, often more than a fair portion
ex: The lion's share of the budget goes to salaries and health insurance.
Kwame did the lion's share of the cooking for the family reunion.

cloze.s: Although five people worked on the project, the director took the ___ of the credit.

note: In the fable the lion takes everything; today the phrase usually just means the biggest portion.

story: In Irish folklore, a banshee (from the Irish for “woman of the fairy mound”) is a female spirit whose eerie wailing at night warns that someone in the family is about to die.
def: someone or something making a loud, shrill, wailing scream
ex: The toddler screamed like a banshee when it was time to leave the playground.
The wind howled like a banshee through the broken windows of the old farmhouse.

cloze.s: When the fire alarm went off, the old siren wailed like a ___ through the empty halls.

story: In the Book of Job, a righteous man loses his wealth, his children, and his health, yet endures his suffering without abandoning his faith in God, and is eventually restored. The Letter of James later speaks of “the patience of Job.”
def: extraordinary endurance and calm tolerance, especially in the face of repeated trouble or provocation
ex: Teaching a nervous teenager to drive takes the patience of Job.
The customer service rep showed the patience of Job, calmly explaining the refund policy for the fifth time.

cloze.s: Aisha has ___; she sat through four hours of airport delays without a single complaint.

story: In the Book of Exodus, while the Israelites wander in the desert after leaving Egypt, God provides them with manna, a mysterious food that appears on the ground each morning.
def: an unexpected help or benefit that arrives just when it is most needed
ex: The surprise tax refund was manna from heaven for the struggling family.
For the drought-stricken farmers, the week of steady rain was manna from heaven.

cloze.s: After months without work, the freelance contract that showed up in Malik's inbox felt like ___.

story: In the Book of Exodus, God promises to bring the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt into “a land flowing with milk and honey,” describing the fertile, abundant land of Canaan.
def: a place of great abundance, comfort, and opportunity where life is easy
ex: Gold-rush California was advertised as a land of milk and honey, though most miners found little.
Recruiters promised a land of milk and honey, but the overseas jobs paid far less than advertised.

cloze.s: The valley was a true ___: fertile soil, plentiful water, and harvests bigger than anyone could eat.

story: The phrase is usually traced to the Book of Ecclesiastes, which says that dead flies make a perfumer's ointment stink, just as a little folly can spoil a reputation for wisdom.
def: a small flaw or problem that spoils something otherwise good
ex: The new apartment is perfect; the only fly in the ointment is the noisy bar downstairs.
The vacation was wonderful, with one fly in the ointment: Tomás lost his passport.

cloze.s: The picnic was lovely, but the one ___ was the swarm of ants that found our sandwiches.

story: The saying comes from the Book of Ecclesiastes, “there is no new thing under the sun,” part of the Teacher's reflection that what has been will be again.
def: everything that happens or is invented has already happened or existed before in some form
ex: Fashion proves there's nothing new under the sun; bell-bottoms keep coming back.
The scam uses social media, but there's nothing new under the sun; con artists ran the same trick by mail.

cloze.s: The “revolutionary” diet was just fasting with a new name, proof that there's ___.

story: Named for Mercury, the swift Roman messenger god. Through astrology, people born under the planet Mercury were thought to be quick-witted and changeable, which gave the word its modern sense.
def: changing mood or mind suddenly and unpredictably; volatile
ex: The team's mercurial striker can win a game alone or disappear for weeks.
Working for a mercurial boss meant Priya never knew whether a meeting would bring praise or shouting.

cloze.s: The ___ chef was cheerful one minute and throwing pans the next, so the staff tiptoed around him.

note: Can also mean lively and quick-witted, but the “unpredictable” sense is far more common today.

story: In Greek myth, the Hydra of Lerna was a many-headed water serpent; whenever one head was cut off, two grew back. Hercules killed it, with his nephew Iolaus searing the neck stumps with fire so no new heads could grow.
def: a problem with many sources that keeps growing back worse each time one part is dealt with
ex: Spam is a hydra: block one sender and two more appear.
Officials described the smuggling network as a hydra that regrouped after every arrest.

cloze.s: Corruption in the agency proved a ___; every time one official was fired, two others took up the scheme.

note: Often used as an adjective: “a hydra-headed problem.”

story: In Greek myth, the Chimera was a fire-breathing monster that was part lion, part goat, and part serpent. The hero Bellerophon, riding the winged horse Pegasus, killed it.
def: an imagined hope or idea that is impossible to achieve; also, a mix of very different parts
ex: Total job security turned out to be a chimera in the fast-changing tech industry.
The plan for a product that was cheap, fast, and perfect was a chimera from the start.

cloze.s: For years, the dream of a peace deal between the two feuding families proved a ___ that always slipped away.

note: In biology, a chimera is an organism containing cells from two genetically different individuals.

story: In Greek myth, Panacea was a goddess of universal healing, a daughter of Asclepius, the god of medicine; her name means “all-healing.”
def: a solution or remedy that people claim will cure every problem or illness
ex: Technology alone is no panacea for the problems in our schools.
The supplement was marketed as a panacea for everything from headaches to heart disease.

cloze.s: Lower interest rates help, but economists warn they are not a ___ for every weakness in the economy.

note: Usually used skeptically: “no panacea,” “not a panacea.”

story: In Greek myth, the aegis was a protective shield or goatskin cloak carried by Zeus and his daughter Athena, often shown bearing the head of the Gorgon Medusa.
def: the protection, support, or sponsorship of a powerful person or organization
ex: The vaccination campaign was carried out under the aegis of the World Health Organization.
The research center operates under the aegis of the state university.

cloze.s: The peace talks took place under the ___ of the United Nations, which provided security and translators.

note: Almost always appears in the phrase “under the aegis of.”

story: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus must sail through a narrow strait between Scylla, a six-headed monster on a cliff, and Charybdis, a deadly whirlpool; steering away from one meant drifting toward the other.
def: trapped by two dangers, where avoiding one means getting closer to the other
ex: The central bank was caught between Scylla and Charybdis: raise rates and risk recession, or wait and let inflation grow.
Fatima felt stuck between Scylla and Charybdis, choosing between a dull job and a risky startup.

cloze.s: Forced to pick between cutting half the staff and going bankrupt, the owner was steering ___.

syn: between a rock and a hard place
on the horns of a dilemma

story: Ancient Greeks believed that the halcyon, a mythical bird linked with the kingfisher, nested on the sea around the winter solstice and calmed the winds and waves for about two weeks. In one myth, the bird was Alcyone, transformed after her husband drowned.
def: a remembered past period of happiness, peace, and success, often looked back on with nostalgia
ex: Diego often talks about the halcyon days of his college summers on the coast.
Old-timers remember the halcyon days when the factory employed half the town.

cloze.s: Looking back, Maria realized those carefree first years in Lisbon had been the ___ of her life.

story: In the Book of Job, God describes Behemoth, an enormous, powerful land creature, to show Job the greatness of creation; some scholars think the image was based on the hippopotamus or elephant.
def: something enormous and powerful, especially a huge company, organization, or machine
ex: The tiny startup was swallowed up by an e-commerce behemoth.
The new cruise ship is a 20-deck behemoth that dwarfs everything else in the harbor.

cloze.s: The 400-ton mining truck, a steel ___ on wheels, could barely squeeze down the town's main street.

story: In the Hebrew Bible, Leviathan is a monstrous sea serpent or dragon, described in Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. The philosopher Thomas Hobbes later used the name for his 1651 book about the powerful state.
def: something huge and powerful, especially a vast ship, sea creature, or overbearing organization
ex: The container ship, a 400-meter leviathan, blocked the canal for days.
Critics described the merged media company as a leviathan controlling what millions of people watch.

cloze.s: Whale watchers gasped as the blue whale, a ___ longer than their boat, surfaced right beside them.

story: In Genesis, people build a city and a tower reaching toward heaven. God halts the project by making them speak different languages so they can no longer understand each other, and scatters them across the earth.
def: a noisy confusion of many voices or languages; a situation where no one can understand anyone else
ex: The international conference was a Tower of Babel until the interpreters arrived.
The project became a Tower of Babel, with each team using software that couldn't talk to the others.

cloze.s: With twelve languages spoken in the hostel kitchen and none shared by everyone, dinner felt like the ___.

note: The word babble is not derived from Babel; it is a separate word imitating meaningless chatter.

story: In the Book of Daniel, King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great statue with a head of gold but feet of mixed iron and clay. A stone strikes the weak feet and the whole statue shatters.
def: a hidden flaw or weakness in someone who is greatly admired or respected
ex: The scandal revealed that the beloved TV host had feet of clay.
Every hero has feet of clay, Grandma told Jamal when his favorite athlete was caught cheating.

cloze.s: Fans were crushed to learn that their idol, praised for his honesty, had ___ and had lied about his charity work.

note: Unlike Achilles' heel, used mostly of admired people whose character turns out to be flawed.

story: In the Acts of the Apostles, Saul, a persecutor of early Christians, is struck by a blinding light on the road to Damascus and hears the voice of Jesus. He converts and becomes the apostle Paul.
def: a sudden, dramatic change of mind or belief, often a complete reversal
ex: After his heart attack, Liam had a road-to-Damascus moment and quit smoking for good.
Reading her late father's letters was a road-to-Damascus experience that changed how Olga saw her family.

cloze.s: The lifelong meat lover had a ___ moment after touring a factory farm and became a vegetarian overnight.

note: Often used as an adjective, “a road-to-Damascus moment”; the related phrase is “a Damascene conversion.”

story: In the Book of Exodus, while Moses is on Mount Sinai receiving the law, the Israelites persuade his brother Aaron to make a calf of gold, which they worship as an idol. Moses destroys it when he returns.
def: something, especially money or material success, that is wrongly worshipped or valued above everything else
ex: The film criticizes a culture that bows down to the golden calf of celebrity.
For some executives, the quarterly stock price has become a golden calf.

cloze.s: The preacher warned that wealth had become the town's ___, worshipped more devotedly than any faith.

story: In Greek myth, Proteus was a sea god who could change his shape at will to escape capture. In the Odyssey, Menelaus holds on to him as he turns into a lion, a serpent, water, and a tree, until Proteus answers his questions.
def: able to change form or adapt easily to many different roles or situations; very versatile
ex: The protean actor played a villain, a comic, and a romantic lead all in one year.
Jazz is a protean art form, constantly absorbing new styles.

cloze.s: Her ___ talent let her switch from writing novels to directing films to composing music with ease.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus says, “neither cast ye your pearls before swine,” warning against offering something precious to those who will not value it.
def: something valuable offered to people who are unable or unwilling to appreciate it
ex: Serving the vintage wine at the rowdy tailgate party was casting pearls before swine.
Fatima felt her detailed talk on Renaissance art was pearls before swine to the bored tourists.

cloze.s: Explaining fine cheese to my brother, who only eats processed slices, is like casting ___.

story: In the Gospel of Luke, Jesus quotes this proverb, predicting that the people of his hometown, Nazareth, will demand he perform for them the miracles he performed elsewhere.
def: a reminder to fix your own faults before criticizing or correcting those of other people
ex: The disorganized consultant lecturing us about time management needed to hear “physician, heal thyself.”
Before scolding the kids about screen time, Dad muttered, “Physician, heal thyself,” and put down his phone.

cloze.s: The financial adviser was drowning in credit card debt, so his advice on saving invited a quick ___ from his clients.

story: In the Hebrew Bible, people mourning or repenting dressed in sackcloth, a coarse, rough fabric, and put ashes on themselves; in the Book of Jonah, even the king of Nineveh does so.
def: a public display of deep regret, apology, or humiliation for wrongdoing
ex: After the data leak, the company's CEO appeared in sackcloth and ashes, promising sweeping reforms.
Malik didn't need to put on sackcloth and ashes; a simple apology for forgetting the date would do.

cloze.s: The team's owner came before the fans in ___, admitting that the trades had been a disaster.

story: In the First Book of Kings, two women claim the same baby. King Solomon orders the child cut in two to share; when one woman begs him to give the baby to the other instead, he knows she is the real mother.
def: showing great wisdom and fairness in judging or settling a difficult dispute
ex: The judge's Solomonic ruling let both parents share custody of the family dog.
Facing two equally strong candidates, the committee reached a Solomonic compromise and created a second position.

cloze.s: Splitting the inheritance so each brother got the part he valued most was a truly ___ solution.

story: In the Book of Genesis, Methuselah, the grandfather of Noah, is said to have lived 969 years, the longest life recorded in the Bible.
def: a person or thing that is extremely old
ex: At 45, the veteran quarterback is the Methuselah of the league.
Our 1998 laptop is a Methuselah of a machine, but it still turns on.

cloze.s: The bristlecone pine, which can live nearly 5,000 years, is the ___ of the plant world.

story: In the Book of Jonah, the prophet flees God's command by ship. When a violent storm strikes, the sailors decide Jonah is the cause and throw him overboard, where he is swallowed by a great fish.
def: a person believed to bring bad luck to those around them
ex: Superstitious sailors once called an unlucky crewmate a Jonah.
After three losses in a row whenever he attended, Tomás worried he was a Jonah for his team.

cloze.s: Every project the new manager touched went wrong, and coworkers began whispering that he was a ___.

story: In Genesis, after Cain murders his brother Abel, God sentences him to wander the earth and places a mark on him so that no one who finds him will kill him.
def: a sign of disgrace or shame that brands someone as guilty, especially of a serious crime
ex: For years, the false accusation followed him like the mark of Cain.
In the novel, the deserter's scar is a mark of Cain that everyone in the village recognizes.

cloze.s: Even after his name was cleared, the fraud scandal stayed with the banker like the ___, and clients never trusted him again.

note: In Genesis the mark protected Cain, but English uses the phrase for a stigma of guilt.

story: The word comes from the prophet Jeremiah, whose biblical book warns of disaster and mourns the coming destruction of Jerusalem; the Book of Lamentations is traditionally credited to him as well.
def: a long, mournful complaint or angry speech warning about decline and coming disaster
ex: The columnist's latest jeremiad blamed smartphones for the decline of civilization.
Grandpa launched into a jeremiad about how nobody writes letters anymore.

cloze.s: The retiring professor's farewell speech became a twenty-minute ___ about the collapse of reading among students.

story: In the Book of Judges, the Gileadites caught fleeing Ephraimites by making them say “shibboleth.” The Ephraimites pronounced it “sibboleth,” revealing who they were.
def: a word, custom, or belief that marks someone as belonging to a group, or an outdated belief held without question
ex: Knowing the right jargon is a shibboleth that separates insiders from outsiders in the art world.
The old shibboleth that tea must be made with boiling water was challenged by the tasting panel.

cloze.s: For locals, pronouncing the town's name correctly is a ___ that instantly reveals who grew up there.

story: In a fable traditionally credited to Aesop, a dog lies in a manger full of hay and snarls to keep a hungry ox from eating it, even though the dog cannot eat hay itself.
def: a person who selfishly keeps others from having something even though they have no use for it themselves
ex: Liam was a dog in the manger, refusing to lend his unused tent to his sister.
Critics accused the company of a dog-in-the-manger strategy, buying patents it never planned to use just to block rivals.

cloze.s: Hannah never rides her old bike but won't let her brother borrow it; she's a real ___.

story: In Aesop's fable “The Man and the Satyr,” a satyr sees a traveler blow on his hands to warm them and then on his soup to cool it. Distrustful of anyone who can blow hot and cold from the same mouth, the satyr wants nothing more to do with him.
def: to keep changing one's attitude or opinion, being enthusiastic one moment and uninterested the next
ex: Investors blew hot and cold on the project, pledging money one week and pulling out the next.
Wei is tired of dating someone who blows hot and cold about their future together.

cloze.s: The client keeps ___ about the redesign, loving it on Monday and rejecting it on Friday.

story: In Hans Christian Andersen's tale, a queen tests whether a stranger is a true princess by hiding a single pea under twenty mattresses. When the girl complains of a sleepless, bruising night, her extreme sensitivity proves she is royal.
def: a person who is extremely sensitive to small discomforts or very hard to please
ex: Sofia is a real princess and the pea; she can't sleep if there's a single crease in the sheets.
The fussy hotel guest was a princess-and-the-pea type who complained about the thread count.

cloze.s: My brother complains if a restaurant chair is even slightly wobbly; he's a total ___.

story: In the tale of Aladdin, added to the Arabian Nights by its 18th-century French translator Antoine Galland, a sorcerer sends young Aladdin into an underground cave filled with jeweled fruit and treasure to fetch a magic lamp.
def: a place crammed with many valuable, surprising, or interesting things
ex: Her grandfather's attic was an Aladdin's cave of old maps, coins, and radios.
The tiny shop turned out to be an Aladdin's cave for vintage-guitar collectors.

cloze.s: The flea market was an ___ of antiques, rare records, and forgotten toys.

note: More common in British English, often describing a cluttered shop full of treasures.

story: In an old fable often credited to Aesop, mice meet to decide how to protect themselves from a cat, and one proposes tying a bell around its neck. Everyone agrees it is a fine plan until an old mouse asks who will do it.
def: to take on a risky task for a group's good that everyone agrees is needed but nobody wants to do
ex: Everyone hated the new policy, but no one wanted to bell the cat by raising it with the CEO.
Finally Kwame belled the cat and told the landlord the tenants wouldn't pay the increase.

cloze.s: The whole team agreed the deadline was impossible, but someone still had to ___ and tell the demanding client.

story: In Jewish folklore, a golem is a figure of clay brought to life by mystical means. The best-known legend tells of Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague creating one in the 1500s to protect the city's Jews; in many versions it grows dangerous and must be deactivated.
def: a mindless, robotlike servant, or a creation that grows beyond its maker's control
ex: Some critics fear that powerful AI could become a golem its creators cannot control.
The overgrown bureaucracy had become a golem, mindlessly following rules no one remembered the reason for.

cloze.s: In the science-fiction novel, the lab's obedient clay ___ eventually turns against the scientist who built it.

story: In Norse myth, Valhalla is the god Odin's great hall in Asgard, where warriors who died bravely in battle are brought by the Valkyries to feast and fight until the final battle, Ragnarok.
def: a place of honor or heavenly reward, especially one where the heroes of a field are celebrated
ex: For a baseball player, the Hall of Fame in Cooperstown is a kind of Valhalla.
The museum is a Valhalla of classic race cars, each with a famous history.

cloze.s: The old veterans liked to imagine their fallen comrades feasting together in a warriors' ___.

story: In Greek myth, Procrustes was a bandit who forced travelers to lie on his bed, stretching those who were too short and cutting the legs of those too tall so that they fit it exactly. The hero Theseus killed him the same way.
def: forcing everything to fit a single rigid standard, ignoring individual differences or circumstances
ex: Teachers criticized the Procrustean testing system that judged every child by the same narrow scores.
The company's Procrustean dress code ignored the needs of workers in the hot warehouse.

cloze.s: Squeezing every patient into the same fifteen-minute slot is a ___ approach that ignores how different cases are.

story: For one of his twelve labors, Hercules had to clean, in a single day, the stables of King Augeas, where great herds had left filth piling up for many years. He did it by diverting two rivers through them.
def: a place or system so dirty or corrupt that cleaning it up seems almost impossible
ex: The new commissioner vowed to clean out the Augean stables of the corrupt city department.
Tackling his teenage son's bedroom felt like cleaning the Augean stables.

cloze.s: Investigators said reforming the scandal-ridden agency would be like cleaning the ___.

story: In Greek myth, the Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity. As punishment, Zeus chained him to a rock where an eagle ate his liver each day, and it grew back each night.
def: boldly creative, inventive, or daring, especially in defying limits to benefit people
ex: The scientist's Promethean ambition was to bring cheap clean energy to every village on earth.
Critics praised the composer's Promethean energy, which produced three symphonies in a single year.

cloze.s: The inventor's ___ vision of bringing electric light to every home seemed to challenge the very limits of nature.

story: In Homer's Iliad, Stentor was a Greek herald whose voice was as loud as the voices of fifty men combined.
def: extremely loud and powerful, especially describing a speaking voice
ex: The drill sergeant's stentorian voice carried across the entire parade ground.
The auctioneer called out the bids in a stentorian tone that needed no microphone.

cloze.s: Without a microphone, the tour guide relied on her ___ voice to reach the back of the crowded cathedral.

story: Janus was the Roman god of doorways, gates, and beginnings, shown with two faces looking in opposite directions, toward the past and the future.
def: deceitful and hypocritical, or having two sharply contrasting sides or aspects
ex: The Janus-faced manager praised the plan in meetings while quietly working to kill it.
Social media is Janus-faced, connecting distant friends while also spreading misinformation.

cloze.s: The ___ diplomat assured both rival nations of his full support while secretly favoring neither.

story: In Homer's Odyssey, some of Odysseus's men eat the lotus fruit offered by the Lotus-Eaters, lose all desire to return home, and have to be dragged back to the ships.
def: a person who lives in lazy, dreamy pleasure and has lost interest in work or responsibilities
ex: After moving to the island, Diego became a lotus-eater, spending his days in a hammock.
The resort's spa packages are designed to turn busy executives into happy lotus-eaters for a week.

cloze.s: Her parents worried that after a year of beach life, she had become a ___ with no plans to return to college.
